name: Cathedral Traverse (Teewinot, Owen, Grand Teton)

legs.route: Ridge traverse over the top, passed on its north side
legs.connect: Drop west from Teewinot through notches and a snowfield, then follow a flat bench to the next summit; a chimney downclimb or rappels gets you off its far side.
Cross a small ridge hump on its north side over loose ledges and sometimes steep snow, finishing on easy fifth class.
Cross steep snow to the base of the Owen climb; Owen is reached by its chimney system, and the route is easy to lose.

legs.route: North Ridge (Italian Cracks), via Gunsight Notch and the Grandstand
legs.connect: Descend gullies from Owen's shoulder with several rappels into the notch, climb out via a 5.7 pitch up the Grandstand, then fourth class to the North Ridge.

how: This is the northern half of the Grand Traverse and is far more commonly done than the full thing. Climbers start in the dark from the valley to reach Teewinot at first light, then follow the crest south over two minor summits to Owen. The crux is leaving Owen: a long descent with several rappels into Gunsight Notch, then roped climbing up the Grandstand and the Grand's North Ridge (sections of 5.5 to 5.7, a 5.8 grade overall). Expect snow and ice on the Owen section early in the season.
descent: Come down the Grand by the Owen-Spalding route (third class with rappels), continue to the Lower Saddle, and walk out Garnet Canyon, which is long and tiring at the end of the day.
logistics: One 60 m rope handles the rappels. Water is scarce except where snow remains; refill on Owen if possible and at the Lower Saddle. Guided trips typically run mid-August to early September.
notes: Source of the leg order: a first-person trip report (Teewinot, 11,840, East Prong, Owen, Grandstand, North Ridge) and the Grand Traverse write-up (Italian Cracks 5.7). The trip report quotes 5.5-5.7 on the ridge plus a 5.9 chimney nearby; kept the higher grade for the overall grade only as the headline 5.8 from a third page. Time given in one report (26 hours in deep snow) is not typical.

name: Grand Traverse (Teewinot to Nez Perce)

legs.connect: Optional intermediate summit; west side descends by rappel or downclimb.
Optional intermediate summit; traverse mostly on its north side, drop west by rappel or a 5.4 downclimb.
Climb a corkscrew chimney system that is easy to miss; leave packs on the shoulder.

legs.route: Italian Cracks on the North Ridge
legs.connect: Descend gullies from Owen's shoulder with several rappels into Gunsight Notch, then two or three pitches out of it.
Down the Owen-Spalding route to the Lower Saddle, then the Southwest Couloir to the col with Middle Teton.
Cross the Middle-South col and climb third class; descend the East Ridge (fourth class).
Follow the ridge east from South Teton; downclimb the east face at third class.
Traverse around an intervening feature; short rappels are possible.
Descend Gilkey's east face at third class; cross a snowfield if it is present.
Descend Spalding's east ridge and stay on the crest.

legs.route: Northwest Couloir (fourth class with a low fifth crux)
legs.connect: Descend Cloudveil's east ridge to a col, then contour on the north side to the couloir.

how: A twelve-summit ridge enchainment from Teewinot to Nez Perce covering the whole skyline, graded V at 5.7 to 5.8 on rock. Climbers go north to south, with the first half the hardest to route-find (Gunsight Notch is the crux) and the second half long, repetitive scrambling and short rappels. Counts of summits vary: Peak 11,840 and East Prong are often treated as optional or not counted. Many parties rappel about a dozen times, though most can be downclimbed.
descent: From Nez Perce, reverse the couloir and scramble talus down to the Garnet Canyon trail, then hike out to the valley trailhead.
logistics: Water is reliable only near the Lower Saddle until Garnet Canyon is reached again after Nez Perce. A bivy site sits at the Middle-South col for two-day attempts. The usual window is mid-summer to early fall, with early-season snow demanding crampons on the Owen section.
notes: Summit count disagrees across sources (10 vs 12); other accounts omit Peak 11,840 and East Prong. The first complete traverse in 1963 went the opposite direction (Nez Perce to Teewinot) and ended on Teewinot; north-to-south is now usual. Grades kept at the higher quoted values (5.8).

name: Middle Teton and South Teton

legs.connect: Drop back to the col between the two peaks and cross a flat spot to the base of the couloir.

how: Both peaks are climbed from one meadow camp or in a single day from the valley by way of the South Fork of Garnet Canyon, up talus and snowfields to the col between them. From the col each peak is a short out-and-back; the order varies, with the Middle Teton couloir containing the hardest moves, two class 4 steps and loose rock above a big drop. Climbers usually carry an ice axe and may need crampons or spikes on the snowfields early in the season.
descent: Return to the col, then retrace the moraine, talus and snow to the meadows and walk the Garnet Canyon trail out. The descent of the Middle Teton couloir is slower than the climb.
logistics: Day trip from the valley trailhead is roughly 15 miles and about 7,000 feet of gain. The meadows have water to refill. Camping needs a backcountry permit.
notes: Summit order differs: one report climbs the South Teton first, the route description the Middle first. Both are valid. Class of the couloirs is not agreed; kept the class 4 steps from the trip report.

name: Cirque of the Towers Traverse

legs.route: Optional side summit via short rappels from the Pingora col
legs.connect: Optional; two short rappels off the west side.
Rappel from Pingora to the col with Tiger Tower or Wolf's Head and follow the crest.
Scramble from the Wolf's Head col; rappel the southwest face afterward.

legs.route: Thoroughfare to the north summit, then the summit traverse (5.8)
legs.connect: Cross the col from Overhanging Tower.
Three long rappels to the col.

legs.route: Loose third class to the shoulder and summit
legs.connect: Three long rappels from Block Tower to the next col.
Optional South Watchtower on third class on the way.

legs.route: Ridge via Warrior II and Warrior I
legs.connect: Follow saddles over the two Warriors; beware a false summit.

duration: 1 long day from camp, or 2 days
how: A roughly four-mile granite ridge starting at Pingora and ending on Warbonnet, rated IV 5.9 with about 17 rappels in total. The rock climbing is concentrated on Pingora, Wolf's Head and Shark's Nose; the rest is third-class scrambling and downclimbing. Parties often rope only the harder sections and move together elsewhere, which demands competence on exposed ground. Watch for afternoon storms: the scrambling is dangerous when wet.
descent: From Warbonnet, descend the south slopes to the gully between it and Sundance, drop to the trail and walk back to camp.
logistics: Long hike in from the Big Sandy trailhead, about 10 miles each way. A single rack to #3, shoulder slings and a 60 m rope or longer are the norm. Water is scarce on the ridge, and snow lingers in cols early in the season.
notes: The 1960s account ends at Pylon Peak (and mentions Warbonnet in its opening); the modern write-up includes the Warriors and Warbonnet. Overall grade IV 5.9 from the full-traverse report; the older report gave IV F7. Pingora and Wolf's Head are rock climbs, which sit at the edge of the 'alpine' scope; kept because this is a ridge traverse of named summits.
